vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: The shop where you buy food for the house
An outdoor meal where the food is cooked on a grill
The food that is still there after the meal
Made at home, not bought ready
A simple American restaurant, open most of the day
The amount of food served to one person
A small amount of food between meals
A meal where every guest brings a dish

vocab.text: Two invitations that mean very different things. A potluck asks you to arrive with a dish for everybody; a cookout only asks you to arrive. If you are not sure which one you have been invited to, ask what you can bring. Nobody is ever offended by that question.

paras: The first thing a visitor notices in the United States is the portion. A single plate at a diner often holds enough food for two people, and nobody expects you to finish it. That is why the box for the leftovers is not embarrassing: it is part of the system, and the server offers it before you ask. The second thing is how much of the week is planned around the grocery store, where a family buys food for seven days at a time and the snacks take up an entire aisle.

Then come the invitations, and they are not the same. A cookout means somebody is cooking outside and you bring nothing but yourself. A potluck means every guest arrives with a dish, and there is an unwritten rule that homemade beats bought. If you do not know how many people are coming, ask, because the number changes what you make. And if you do not have much time, ask what is missing: there are usually not enough salads and there is always too much dessert.

choices: What a visitor has to understand about portions, shopping and invitations in the United States

items: Taking the leftovers home is considered rude in the United States.
The text says the box is part of the system and the server offers it before you ask.
At a cookout every guest has to bring a dish.
The text says a cookout means you bring nothing but yourself. That is the potluck.

practice.title: Turn each cue into a full sentence. Use the quantifier in brackets.

items.situation: A colleague invites you to something on Saturday and does not say whether to bring food.
tips: Ask what you can bring, not whether you should.
One of the two words names an invitation where everybody cooks.

items.situation: The plate at the diner is twice the size you expected.
tips: There is a word for what stays on the plate.
Ask for the box before the server clears the table.

items.situation: You are cooking for a potluck and you do not know the numbers.
tips: People are countable, food is not.
Two different question words, one for each.

items.situation: Somebody asks whether there is bread in the house and there is none.
tips: Negative sentences do not take some.
One word covers both countable and uncountable here.

items.situation: You want to say the salads ran out but there is far too much dessert.
tips: Enough and too much go with different kinds of noun.
Say both halves in one sentence.

answerkey.title: Reveal the model answers
list: There are a lot of leftovers in the fridge.
We do not have any bread in the house.
How much food should I bring to a potluck?
How many people are coming to the cookout?
answerkey.note: These are models, not the only correct answers. Any natural sentence with the right quantifier works.

listenings.text: Hi Thiago, it is Linda. About Saturday: it is a potluck, not a cookout, so everybody brings something. There are about fifteen of us, and we do not have any dessert yet, so do not bring one, we already have too much sugar in this office. If you want to make something homemade, bring a salad, because there are never enough of those. Do not worry about the amount: whatever is left, people take the leftovers home. See you at one.

Welcome to the store guide. If this is your first time with us, here is how it works. Fresh food is on your right and the frozen aisles are at the back. There are a lot of offers this week on fruit and vegetables, and there is not much left of the bread by six in the evening, so come early for that. Snacks are in aisle four, and yes, it is a whole aisle. If you cannot find something, ask any member of staff. We are open until eleven every day.

extra_audio.text: First, Linda calls Thiago and explains that Saturday is a potluck. Then he asks how many people are coming and how much food he should bring. After that, he goes to the grocery store and buys what is missing. Next, he makes a homemade salad, because there are never enough of those. Finally, everybody takes the leftovers home in a box.
